## Today's Agenda

- What you walk out with today: a topic, search terms, and a search log
- Why a literature review is a map, not a reading list
- Three phases of searching: broad, systematic, and by citation
- Booking your librarian meeting, and what to ask
- Searching in here, then committing your work to GitHub

## What You Walk Out With Today

- A topic, a set of search terms that actually work, and the start of a search log
- That log is most of the Librarian Visit Report
- **No librarian is coming to us.** You book your own appointment at Lovejoy and go to them, and that meeting is the assignment
- Today is how you arrive there with something worth their time
- **Have a topic in mind.** A rough one is fine

## Thirty Sources in an Hour

- You find one article that looks right, and it cites twelve others
- You chase three of those, and each cites fifteen more
- An hour later you have thirty sources open and no idea which one to read first
- The instinct is to retreat: narrow the topic, keep three recent articles, and hope
- That instinct is reasonable, and following it is what makes the next three weeks harder than they need to be

## A Review Is a Map, Not a Reading List

- A **literature review** is not evidence that you read enough articles
- It is a map of who has said what, and where the arguments are
- Think of it as walking into a debate that has been running for years
    - Say your piece cold and you get told it was answered in 2012
    - Knowing the terrain is how you earn the right to ask your question
- You cannot map terrain from three landmarks, which is why retreating to three articles fails

## What a Review Does for You

- **It shows where your work sits.** You are not the first person to wonder this
- **It finds the gap**, which is your answer to "so what?"
- **It stops you rebuilding something that already exists.** Your original idea may be somebody's dissertation from five years ago
- **It hands you methods**: validated measures, sampling strategies, and other people's documented limitations (Krippendorff, 2018; Neuendorf, 2017)
- **It sharpens the question** from "something about Twitch chat" into something you can actually answer

## Exercise: Write Your Search Terms {.discuss}

Answer each in writing, because your librarian will ask you for them:

- Name a media topic you are curious about, in one sentence
- List the words a scholar would use for it that you would not
- Name where you would look first, and state how you would know if you had missed the main body of work

## Phase One: Search Broadly

- Start wide. You are answering basic questions, not finding your final sources
- Ask which words scholars use for this, who keeps coming up, and which journals publish it
- **Google Scholar** comes first. It is less thorough than the real databases, and it is fast and free
- **Wikipedia** is not citable, and its reference list is still a doorway
- Collect anything promising in **Zotero** and tag freely. Do not tidy yet

## Phase Two: Search Systematically

Now you want coverage rather than speed, which means the real databases:

- **Communication & Mass Media Complete** is the main one for our field
- **PsycINFO** fits a question that touches emotion, persuasion, or cognition
- **Web of Science** and **Scopus** track citations across disciplines

These databases do not work like Google. They expect **Boolean operators**, which the next
slide explains.

## Building a Search String

- **AND** narrows, so both terms must appear. **OR** widens. **NOT** excludes
- An asterisk is a wildcard: `stream*` catches stream, streams, streaming, and streamer

```
(livestream* OR "live streaming" OR Twitch) AND
(motivation* OR gratification* OR engagement) AND
(viewer* OR audience* OR chat)
```

- The string has three concept blocks joined with AND, each holding its own synonyms
- Build yours the same way and take it with you: a librarian can fix a string like this in seconds

## Keep a Search Log

Keep it as plain text in your repository. For every search you run, write down:

- The date and which database
- The exact string, copied and pasted, never remembered
- The limiters you set and how many results came back
- How many results you kept

**You should see** it getting boring to write, which is the point. The log lets you defend
the strategy later, and it shows you fast which searches are not working.

## Phase Three: Follow the Citations

- Pick a few **keystone articles**, the ones that clearly sit at the center
- **Backward chaining:** read what they cite, which takes you to the foundations
- **Forward chaining:** use Google Scholar's "Cited by" to see who has cited them since, which shows you how the argument moved
- The search snowballs on purpose, following the network out from what matters most rather than wandering

## Knowing When to Stop

**Saturation** is the point where more searching stops changing your understanding. You will
recognize it three ways:

- Three database searches in a row turn up nothing new that is relevant
- New articles keep citing the same eight or ten sources you have already read
- You can guess what an article says from its title and abstract

Saturation does not mean you read everything. It means you stop searching and start
synthesizing.

## Book Your Librarian Appointment Today

- Go to [Lovejoy Library](https://www.siue.edu/lovejoy-library/) and ask for the **Mass Communications subject librarian** by name. That is what they are there for
- Book it **this week**, because the report is due Friday, September 18, and their calendar is not yours
- Bring your topic, your terms, and your search log
    - A consultation with nothing in hand wastes the half hour and gives you nothing to write up
- The librarian gives you what a chapter cannot: the interface, the limiters, and the tricks that only come from using these every day

## What to Ask While You Are There

- Which database is actually right for **my** question?
- How do I get the full text when the library does not subscribe?
- How do I set up a saved search and an alert for new results?
- What is the fastest way to push a batch of results into Zotero?
- How do I use interlibrary loan? It is free and much faster than you expect

## Search in Here, Now

- Open a database and run your first real string
- Start the search log on your **first** search, not once you have something good
- Before you leave, have a topic, one string that works, and three sources in Zotero
- Bring me the search that returns 40,000 hits, or the one that returns none. Both are normal, and both are fixable in about a minute

## Last Part of Today: Commit Your Work

- You have a topic, a working string, and the start of a search log, and none of it is anywhere but your laptop
- Download this file into the **top folder** of your workspace, beside `README.md`:
  [aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/starters/01-commit-your-work.qmd](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/starters/01-commit-your-work.qmd)
- **Getting that file onto GitHub is the check.** It is not in the template, so if I can see it in your repository, you put it there yourself

## Save, Stage, Commit, Push

1. **Save** it with `Ctrl+S`. The dot in the tab turns back into an X
2. Open **Source Control** in the left bar, or press `Ctrl+Shift+G`. Your file is listed with a **U**
3. **Stage** it: hover over the name and click the **+**. It moves to Staged Changes
4. Type a **message** a stranger could read, then click **Commit**. Never write "update"
5. Click **Sync Changes**. The first time from a folder it says **Publish Branch** instead

**You should see** the file on your repository page at github.com when you refresh it. A
commit stays on your laptop, and the push is what sends it. You need both, every time.
